title: Musk and Huang Unite Behind Open-Weight AI as Industry Coalition Swells to 77
excerpt: What began as Jensen Huang's first-ever X post has grown into a sweeping industry push urging Washington to treat open AI models as a strategic asset, not a security risk.
body:
• A coalition led by Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta published "Open Weights and American AI Leadership" on July 24, urging Washington to avoid premature restrictions on downloadable AI models.
  • Signatories doubled from 25 to 50 within a day and reached 77 by July 27, with OpenAI, Google, AMD, Cisco, SpaceX, and GitHub joining — only Anthropic declined to sign.
  • Elon Musk endorsed Jensen Huang's first-ever X post promoting the letter, writing "This has my full support."
  • The push comes as US policymakers weigh restrictions on Chinese AI models, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warning of potential sanctions over intellectual property theft.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang chose a policy letter — not a product launch — for his debut on X. On July 24, he published "Open Weights and American AI Leadership," a three-page document arguing that the United States cannot maintain its AI dominance without embracing open-weight models that anyone can download, inspect, and run.

Within hours, Elon Musk had thrown his weight behind the effort. "This has my full support," Musk posted. The endorsement from two of technology's most powerful figures marked a striking moment of alignment between executives whose companies — Tesla, xAI, and Nvidia — are deeply intertwined across AI infrastructure, autonomous vehicles, and robotics.

A Coalition That Keeps Growing

The letter initially carried 25 signatures, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Dell Technologies, Palantir, Hugging Face, Mistral, Andreessen Horowitz, Y Combinator, Perplexity, ServiceNow, CrowdStrike, and the Linux Foundation. By Monday, July 27, the list had swelled to 77 organizations. OpenAI formally joined, with CEO Sam Altman writing: "I want the US to win in AI both in open source and proprietary models." Google's Sundar Pichai endorsed it on behalf of the company. Microsoft's Satya Nadella called open-weight models "essential to a healthy AI ecosystem."

"AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty."

— Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO, in his first X post

The China Factor

The coalition's urgency is shaped by Washington's growing concern about Chinese AI models. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released in July, demonstrated that Chinese startups can match some American models on benchmarks. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that the Trump administration would review whether Chinese companies were stealing American intellectual property, warning the government has "the ability to sanction them because of this theft."

The open-letter signatories are pushing back against broad restrictions. They argue that open-weight models — which make their trained parameters available for download — strengthen competition and ensure AI benefits are "broadly shared rather than concentrated in a few hands." The implicit message: heavy-handed regulation would hurt American competitiveness more than it would contain Chinese AI development.

The One Holdout

Anthropic was the most notable absence from the coalition. CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post that Anthropic has never sought to ban open-weight models but argued that restricting the most powerful chips — predominantly made by Nvidia — in places like China remains the better approach to limiting dangerous AI development. He also advocated for punishing foreign model makers that use Western AI outputs for large-scale training.

Nvidia's Expanding AI Empire

The open-weight push is part of Nvidia's broader strategy to position itself at the centre of AI infrastructure. Beyond the policy letter, Nvidia is reportedly in talks to provide a financing guarantee of up to $250 billion to help OpenAI lease a $500 billion computing hub that SoftBank is developing in Ohio. The company also announced a $5 billion investment in Ilya Sutskever's Safe Superintelligence, one of the chipmaker's largest funding deals of the AI boom.

Huang and Musk have a long collaborative history. Their relationship dates back to at least 2016, when Musk personally emailed Huang requesting an early unit of Nvidia's DGX-1 AI supercomputer for OpenAI. More recently, Nvidia's GPUs power both Tesla's autonomous driving systems and xAI's Grok models. In November 2025, the pair shared a stage at a US-Saudi Investment Forum, where they announced a 500-megawatt AI data centre project with Saudi-backed Humain.

Skepticism Beneath the Surface

Not everyone is convinced the coalition's enthusiasm will translate into action. Fast Company noted the irony that Meta — a key signatory — has largely moved away from open models after the demise of its Llama line, placing its bets on massive closed models through Meta Superintelligence Labs. The economics of frontier AI development make closed weights increasingly attractive to investors who expect returns on billions in capital.

For now, the letter represents the AI industry's most unified policy statement to date. Whether Washington listens — and whether the signatories practise what they preach — will shape the next chapter of AI development.
